Feb 25, 2026 Harish G 18 min read INVESTIGATIVE ANALYSIS 
            <h1 class="article-title">Silicon Under Siege: The $52B Ransomware Blind Spot in the CHIPS Act</h1>
            <p class="article-excerpt">The United States is investing $52.7 billion to bring chip manufacturing
                home. Ransomware groups are investing $0 to steal everything those fabs produce. Since 2022,
                cyberattacks targeting the semiconductor industry have surged over 600%, and the CHIPS Act has no
                meaningful answer.</p>

            <img src="/images/articles/semiconductor-ransomware-chips-act-2026.webp"
                alt="Silicon Under Siege: Semiconductor Ransomware vs CHIPS Act" class="article-image"
                loading="lazy">
        </header>

        <div class="article-content">

            <div class="success-box" style="margin-bottom: 2rem;">
                <ul style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin-bottom: 0; padding-left: 1.25rem; line-height: 1.6; font-size: 0.95rem;">
                    <li><strong>What happened:</strong> Semiconductor ransomware attacks increased 600% since 2022.</li><li><strong>Why it matters:</strong> The $52.7B CHIPS Act funds manufacturing but lacks mandated cybersecurity budget.</li><li><strong>Who is at risk:</strong> Global semiconductor supply chains and domestic critical infrastructure.</li><li><strong>What to do:</strong> Mandate OT/IT segmentation and rigorous cybersecurity standards for CHIPS Act funding recipients.</li>
                </ul>
            </div>

            <p style="font-size: 1.25rem; font-weight: 500; color: var(--text-primary); margin-bottom: 2rem;"><em>The United States is spending $52.7 billion to bring semiconductor manufacturing back home, but they forgot one crucial detail: protecting the fabs from ransomware cartels.</em></p>
            <p>Since 2022, ransomware attacks targeting the semiconductor supply chain have surged by an alarming 600%. We are building state-of-the-art infrastructure on top of a fragile, underfunded cybersecurity foundation.</p>

            <!-- Executive Summary -->
            <div class="technical-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Executive Summary</h3>
                
                
                <p><strong>Confidence Level:</strong> High — based on verified financial filings (MKS Instruments,
                    Applied Materials, Microchip Technology), ransomware group leak site claims (confirmed by
                    BleepingComputer, SecurityWeek, The Record), CHIPS Act allocation data (state.gov, NSF.gov), and
                    the CloudSEK "Silicon Under Siege" threat report.</p>
                <p><strong>TLP:</strong> CLEAR</p>
                <p><em>This analysis is based on publicly available sources including CSO Online, SecurityWeek,
                        BleepingComputer, The Record, CloudSEK, the U.S. Department of State, NSF, and CISA as of
                        February 25, 2026. Details may evolve as the Advantest investigation continues.</em></p>
            </div>

            <div class="toc-container"
                style="background: rgba(0, 217, 255, 0.05); padding: 1.5rem; border-radius: 8px; margin-bottom: 2rem; border-left: 3px solid var(--accent-cyan);">
                <h3 style="margin-top: 0; font-size: 1.2rem; color: var(--text-primary);"><i
                        class="fas fa-list"></i> Table of Contents</h3>
                <ul style="list-style: none; padding-left: 0; margin-bottom: 0;">
                    <li><a href="#the-numbers" style="color: var(--accent-cyan); text-decoration: none;">1. The
                            Numbers: 600% and Counting</a></li>
                    <li><a href="#attack-timeline" style="color: var(--accent-cyan); text-decoration: none;">2. The
                            Attack Timeline: 2023–2026</a></li>
                    <li><a href="#chips-act-gap" style="color: var(--accent-cyan); text-decoration: none;">3. The
                            CHIPS Act Cybersecurity Gap</a></li>
                    <li><a href="#advantest" style="color: var(--accent-cyan); text-decoration: none;">4. The
                            Advantest Mystery</a></li>
                    <li><a href="#supply-chain-cascade" style="color: var(--accent-cyan); text-decoration: none;">5.
                            Supply Chain Cascade: Why One Breach Costs Billions</a></li>
                    <li><a href="#circia" style="color: var(--accent-cyan); text-decoration: none;">6. CIRCIA: The
                            Regulatory Reckoning</a></li>
                    <li><a href="#defense" style="color: var(--accent-cyan); text-decoration: none;">7. Detection
                            and Defense</a></li>
                </ul>
            </div>

            <p>There is a peculiar kind of negligence unique to governments that spend lavishly on building things
                while budgeting nothing to protect them. The United States is in the middle of the most ambitious
                industrial policy experiment since the Apollo program — a $52.7 billion bet, via the <a
                    href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/117th-congress/house-bill/4346" target="_blank"
                    rel="noopener noreferrer">CHIPS and Science Act of 2022</a>, to repatriate semiconductor
                manufacturing from East Asia and secure a domestic supply of the silicon that runs every piece of
                critical infrastructure in the country.</p>

            <p>Meanwhile, ransomware operators have discovered that the semiconductor industry is a spectacularly
                profitable target. According to a <a href="https://www.csoonline.com/" target="_blank"
                    rel="noopener noreferrer">CloudSEK threat report published via CSO Online</a>, titled
                <em>"Silicon Under Siege: The Cyber War Reshaping the Global Semiconductor Industry,"</em>
                cyberattacks targeting the global semiconductor sector have <strong>surged over 600% since
                    2022</strong>. Confirmed ransomware losses in the industry have exceeded <strong>$1.05 billion
                    since 2018</strong>.
            </p>

            <p>The two facts sit next to each other uncomfortably: the largest public investment in semiconductor
                manufacturing in U.S. history is happening at the exact moment the industry is experiencing the
                sharpest escalation of cyberattacks it has ever seen. And they are barely connected.</p>

            <blockquote>
                "We are building the most advanced semiconductor fab in the Western Hemisphere with the
                cybersecurity posture of a regional hospital."
            </blockquote>

            <h2 id="the-numbers">1. The Numbers: 600% and Counting</h2>

            <p>The CloudSEK report puts the scale of the crisis in sharp focus. The semiconductor industry is not
                just one of many sectors dealing with a general uptick in ransomware — it is experiencing a
                <em>targeted escalation</em>.
            </p>

            <p>The drivers are straightforward:</p>

            <ul>
                <li><strong>Geopolitical value:</strong> Semiconductor intellectual property — chip designs, process
                    node secrets, test methodologies — is among the most strategically valuable data on the planet.
                    The U.S.-China semiconductor trade war has intensified the value of this data for state-aligned
                    actors.</li>
                <li><strong>IT/OT convergence:</strong> Modern semiconductor fabrication requires tight integration
                    between information technology (IT) systems and operational technology (OT) systems. CloudSEK's
                    data shows that over 60% of Industrial Control System breaches in the sector originated from IT
                    vulnerabilities — phishing, VPN exploits — before pivoting into operational environments.</li>
                <li><strong>High willingness to pay:</strong> Semiconductor fabs cannot tolerate downtime. A single
                    day of production disruption at a major fab can cost tens of millions of dollars. Ransomware
                    groups know this.</li>
            </ul>

            <h2 id="attack-timeline">2. The Attack Timeline: 2023–2026</h2>

            <p>The following timeline documents every major, publicly confirmed ransomware incident targeting the
                semiconductor supply chain in three years. Every entry has been verified against multiple primary
                sources.</p>

            <table>
                <thead>
                    <tr>
                        <th>Date</th>
                        <th>Target</th>
                        <th>What Happened</th>
                        <th>Confirmed Impact</th>
                        <th>Source</th>
                    </tr>
                </thead>
                <tbody>
                    <tr>
                        <td><strong>Feb 2023</strong></td>
                        <td>MKS Instruments</td>
                        <td>Ransomware attack; operations suspended at multiple facilities. Systems encrypted,
                            employee data potentially exfiltrated (SSNs, bank details).</td>
                        <td>$200M revenue loss (Q1 2023). Downstream impact: Applied Materials reported $250M
                            projected revenue loss from the supply chain disruption.</td>
                        <td><a href="https://www.bankinfosecurity.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">BankInfoSecurity</a>, <a href="https://www.csoonline.com/"
                                target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">CSO Online</a></td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td><strong>Jun 2023</strong></td>
                        <td>Kinmax Technology (TSMC supplier)</td>
                        <td>LockBit ransomware group claimed breach. Kinmax confirmed unauthorized access to its
                            systems. TSMC stated no business data was affected.</td>
                        <td>TSMC confirmed breach was limited to supplier. CloudSEK estimated broader impact at
                            approximately $256M across the supply chain.</td>
                        <td><a href="https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">BleepingComputer</a></td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td><strong>Jan 2024</strong></td>
                        <td>Foxsemicon (Foxconn subsidiary)</td>
                        <td>LockBit ransomware attack. Website defaced with ransom message. Attackers claimed 5 TB
                            of data stolen, including customer and employee information.</td>
                        <td>Company reported no significant operational impact. Website temporarily taken offline.
                        </td>
                        <td><a href="https://www.securityweek.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">SecurityWeek</a>, <a href="https://therecord.media/"
                                target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">The Record</a></td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td><strong>Mar 2024</strong></td>
                        <td>Nexperia</td>
                        <td>Dunghill Leak (Dark Angels) ransomware group. Confirmed unauthorized access to IT
                            servers. 1 TB of data exfiltrated.</td>
                        <td>Stolen data included 371 GB of design/product data (chip schematics, trade secrets,
                            NDAs) and 246 GB of engineering data (manufacturing technologies).</td>
                        <td><a href="https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">BleepingComputer</a>, <a
                                href="https://www.securityweek.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">SecurityWeek</a></td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td><strong>Aug 2024</strong></td>
                        <td>Microchip Technology</td>
                        <td>Play ransomware group. Detected August 17. Systems isolated, production disrupted at
                            multiple facilities.</td>
                        <td>$21.4M in costs (factory underutilization charges). Employee contact info and hashed
                            passwords confirmed exfiltrated. Play published 4 GB data archive.</td>
                        <td><a href="https://www.securityweek.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">SecurityWeek</a>, <a
                                href="https://www.cybersecuritydive.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">Cybersecurity Dive</a></td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td><strong>Feb 2026</strong></td>
                        <td>Advantest Corporation</td>
                        <td>Ransomware detected February 15, 2026. Affected systems isolated. Third-party forensic
                            investigation ongoing.</td>
                        <td>No data breach confirmed as of Feb 25, 2026. No ransomware group has claimed
                            responsibility.</td>
                        <td><a href="https://www.securityweek.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">SecurityWeek</a>, <a
                                href="https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">BleepingComputer</a>, <a
                                href="https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/" target="_blank"
                                rel="noopener noreferrer">Infosecurity Magazine</a></td>
                    </tr>
                </tbody>
            </table>

            <p>The pattern is unmistakable. The interval between major incidents is compressing. The attackers are
                moving up the value chain — from suppliers (MKS, Kinmax) to direct manufacturers (Microchip,
                Nexperia) to the companies that <em>test the chips themselves</em> (Advantest).</p>

            <div class="warning-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Cascading Risk</h3>
                <p style="margin-bottom: 0;">A single attack on MKS Instruments — a <em>supplier</em> — caused
                    Applied Materials to project a <strong>$250 million downstream revenue loss</strong>. The
                    semiconductor supply chain is so tightly coupled that compromising one node can halt production
                    across an entire ecosystem of companies and products.</p>
            </div>

            <h2 id="chips-act-gap">3. The CHIPS Act Cybersecurity Gap</h2>

            <p>The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 is the largest industrial subsidy program the United States has
                enacted in decades. Its stated goal is to reverse America's dependence on East Asian chip
                manufacturing and secure a resilient domestic semiconductor supply.</p>

            <p>Here is where the money goes:</p>

            <table>
                <thead>
                    <tr>
                        <th>Allocation</th>
                        <th>Amount</th>
                        <th>Administered By</th>
                        <th>Purpose</th>
                    </tr>
                </thead>
                <tbody>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Fabrication incentives</td>
                        <td><strong>$39 billion</strong></td>
                        <td>Dept. of Commerce</td>
                        <td>Grants and loans for building new chip fabs on U.S. soil</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>R&D and innovation</td>
                        <td><strong>$11 billion</strong></td>
                        <td>Dept. of Commerce</td>
                        <td>National Semiconductor Technology Center, advanced packaging</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Defense microelectronics</td>
                        <td><strong>$2 billion</strong></td>
                        <td>Dept. of Defense</td>
                        <td>Military-grade chip R&D, university prototyping networks</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Workforce training</td>
                        <td><strong>$200 million</strong></td>
                        <td>National Science Foundation</td>
                        <td>Semiconductor-specific education and training programs</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td style="color: var(--accent-cyan); font-weight: bold;">ITSI Fund (supply chain security)
                        </td>
                        <td style="color: var(--accent-cyan); font-weight: bold;">$500 million</td>
                        <td>Dept. of State</td>
                        <td>International supply chain diversification, secure telecom networks</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>Investment tax credits</td>
                        <td><strong>~$24 billion</strong></td>
                        <td>IRS</td>
                        <td>25% credit for manufacturing equipment costs</td>
                    </tr>
                </tbody>
            </table>

            <p>The only line item that explicitly mentions "security" in the supply chain context is the
                <strong>International Technology Security and Innovation (ITSI) Fund</strong> — $500 million,
                disbursed at <a href="https://www.state.gov/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">$100 million
                    per year over five years through the State Department</a>. This fund is designed for
                <em>international</em> objectives: promoting secure telecom networks in partner countries,
                diversifying the global supply chain, and building testing capacity in allied nations.
            </p>

            <p>It is not designed to help a semiconductor company in Austin, Texas harden its Active Directory
                environment against a Play ransomware intrusion.</p>

            <div class="editorial-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> ⚠️ Editorial Analysis</h3>
                <p>There is a structural assumption embedded in the CHIPS Act: that if the U.S. builds the fabs,
                    cybersecurity will somehow follow. The Commerce Department's $70 billion in received funding
                    requests for the $39 billion fabrication pool suggests the demand vastly exceeds supply — and
                    cybersecurity hardening is not a condition of receiving those funds. Our analysis suggests this
                    creates a scenario where the government is subsidizing the construction of high-value
                    manufacturing targets while providing no proportional funding to defend them against the threat
                    actors who are already, demonstrably, targeting the industry.</p>
            </div>

            <h2 id="advantest">4. The Advantest Mystery</h2>

            <p>On February 15, 2026, Advantest Corporation — a Japanese semiconductor test equipment manufacturer
                headquartered in Tokyo with significant operations in San Jose, California — detected unusual
                activity within its IT network. The company <a href="https://www.securityweek.com/" target="_blank"
                    rel="noopener noreferrer">confirmed it was a ransomware attack</a>, isolated affected systems,
                and engaged third-party forensic investigators.</p>

            <p>As of February 25, 2026:</p>

            <ul>
                <li><strong>No data breach has been confirmed.</strong> Advantest has stated it will notify affected
                    parties if the investigation finds evidence of data exfiltration.</li>
                <li><strong>No ransomware group has claimed responsibility.</strong> This is unusual. Most
                    financially motivated ransomware groups claim victims within 48–72 hours to begin the extortion
                    clock.</li>
                <li><strong>The initial access vector has not been disclosed.</strong></li>
                <li><strong>No significant operational disruption has been reported.</strong></li>
            </ul>

            <p>Advantest is not a household name. But it is a critical node in the global chip supply chain. Their
                automatic test equipment (ATE) is used by <strong>Intel, Samsung, and TSMC</strong> to verify
                semiconductors destined for 5G infrastructure, autonomous vehicles, AI accelerators, and defense
                systems. A sustained disruption to Advantest's operations could create manufacturing bottlenecks
                rippling across the entire chip ecosystem.</p>

            <div class="editorial-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-exclamation-circle"></i> ⚠️ Editorial Analysis: Why No Claim?</h3>
                <p>The absence of a public claim after 10 days is atypical for financially motivated ransomware
                    operators. There are several possible explanations:</p>
                <ul>
                    <li>Active ransom negotiation is underway, and the group is maintaining silence as a condition.
                    </li>
                    <li>The attackers are still performing reconnaissance and exfiltration before deploying their
                        full payload.</li>
                    <li>This is a state-aligned operation where the objective is intelligence collection (IP theft),
                        not extortion. Given the U.S.-China semiconductor export controls, Advantest's test
                        methodology IP would be of significant value to state actors.</li>
                </ul>
                <p style="margin-bottom: 0;"><em>We cannot determine which scenario is in play. This section is
                        speculative analysis, not confirmed intelligence.</em></p>
            </div>

            <h2 id="supply-chain-cascade">5. Supply Chain Cascade: Why One Breach Costs Billions</h2>

            <p>The semiconductor industry operates on a model of extreme interdependence. No single company controls
                the full stack from raw silicon to a finished, tested chip. The supply chain looks roughly like
                this:</p>

            <div class="technical-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-project-diagram"></i> Simplified Semiconductor Supply Chain</h3>
                <pre><code>Raw Materials → Wafer Fabrication → Chip Design (EDA Tools)
 ↓                ↓                    ↓

Equipment Makers → Foundries → Fabless Designers (ASML, Applied (TSMC, Samsung, (AMD, Nvidia, Materials, MKS) Intel, GlobalF) Qualcomm) ↓ Test Equipment → Assembly & Packaging → End Products (Advantest, (ASE, Amkor) (Apple, Dell, Teradyne) Automotive) 

            <p>The MKS Instruments case in 2023 demonstrated exactly how cascading failures work in this model:</p>

            <ol>
                <li><strong>MKS hit by ransomware</strong> → production suspended at their Vacuum Solutions and
                    Photonics Solutions divisions.</li>
                <li><strong>MKS cannot ship components</strong> → Applied Materials (which depends on MKS parts for
                    their equipment) cannot fulfill orders.</li>
                <li><strong>Applied Materials reports $250M revenue impact</strong> from the MKS disruption in their
                    Q2 2023 earnings.</li>
                <li><strong>Fabs waiting for Applied Materials equipment</strong> experience production delays —
                    costs that are never publicly disclosed but are absorbed across the ecosystem.</li>
            </ol>

            <p>One ransomware attack on a component supplier. A quarter-billion-dollar downstream impact on a
                <em>single customer</em>. The total costs across all of MKS's customers were never fully quantified.
            </p>

            <h2 id="circia">6. CIRCIA: The Regulatory Reckoning</h2>

            <p>There is one regulatory mechanism that directly addresses the cybersecurity gap in critical
                manufacturing: the <strong>Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022
                    (CIRCIA)</strong>.</p>

            <p>CIRCIA requires "covered entities" in designated critical infrastructure sectors — including
                <strong>critical manufacturing</strong>, which encompasses semiconductor production — to:
            </p>

            <ul>
                <li>Report significant cyber incidents to CISA within <strong>72 hours</strong>.</li>
                <li>Report ransomware payments to CISA within <strong>24 hours</strong>.</li>
            </ul>

            <p>The final rule is expected to be published by <strong>May 2026</strong>. In preparation, <a
                    href="https://www.cisa.gov/circia" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">CISA and DHS have
                    scheduled sector-specific virtual town halls</a> throughout March 2026:</p>

            <table>
                <thead>
                    <tr>
                        <th>Date</th>
                        <th>Sectors Covered</th>
                    </tr>
                </thead>
                <tbody>
                    <tr>
                        <td>March 12, 2026</td>
                        <td><strong>Critical Manufacturing</strong>, Commercial Facilities, Food &amp; Agriculture
                        </td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>March 19, 2026</td>
                        <td><strong>Defense Industrial Base</strong>, Information Technology</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>March 31, 2026</td>
                        <td>General Session 1</td>
                    </tr>
                    <tr>
                        <td>April 2, 2026</td>
                        <td>General Session 2</td>
                    </tr>
                </tbody>
            </table>

            <p>The <strong>March 12 session on Critical Manufacturing</strong> is directly relevant to every
                semiconductor company operating in the United States. If you are a CISO, compliance officer, or
                security engineer at a semiconductor firm and you are not registered for this session, you should
                be.</p>

            

            <h2 id="defense">7. Detection and Defense</h2>

            <p>Based on the TTPs observed across the semiconductor ransomware incidents documented above, the
                following detection and hardening guidance is applicable to any organization in the semiconductor
                supply chain.</p>

            <h3>7.1 Common Initial Access Vectors</h3>

            <p>Across the documented incidents, the most common initial access methods are:</p>

            <ul>
                <li><strong>Phishing (T1566):</strong> CloudSEK reports that phishing remains the primary initial
                    access vector in over 60% of semiconductor sector breaches.</li>
                <li><strong>VPN and remote access exploitation (T1133):</strong> Exposed management interfaces and
                    VPN appliances with weak or reused credentials.</li>
                <li><strong>Supply chain compromise (T1195):</strong> Attackers targeting smaller suppliers as a
                    pivot into larger firms.</li>
            </ul>

            <h3>7.2 Example Sigma Detection Rule</h3>

            <p>The following rule targets lateral movement patterns consistent with the pre-ransomware
                reconnaissance observed in the Microchip Technology (Play) and MKS Instruments incidents.</p>

            <div class="technical-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-code"></i> Example Detection Rule — Suspicious Remote Service Installation</h3>
                <pre><code class="language-yaml">title: Suspicious Remote Service Installation (Pre-Ransomware Lateral Movement)

id: 8f3c7e91-semiconductor-defense-2026 status: experimental description: > Detects PsExec-style remote service creation commonly used by Play, LockBit, and other ransomware groups during pre-deployment lateral movement — consistent with TTPs observed in semiconductor sector incidents (2023-2026). NOTE: This is an example detection rule engineered from public TTP analysis. It is NOT sourced from any specific vendor. logsource: product: windows service: system detection: selection: EventID: 7045 ServiceName|contains: - ‘PSEXESVC’ - ‘CSEXECSVC’ - ‘paexec’ - ‘remcom’ filter_legitimate: ServiceName|contains: - ‘Windows Update’ - ‘Microsoft’ condition: selection and not filter_legitimate falsepositives: - Legitimate SCCM or endpoint management deployments - Authorized PsExec usage by IT admins (should be whitelisted) level: high tags: - attack.execution - attack.t1569.002 - attack.lateral_movement - attack.t1021.002

SIEM correlation note: For higher-fidelity detection, correlate this rule with Windows Security log EventID 4624 (LogonType 3 — network logon) occurring within 5 minutes on the same host. This correlation must be implemented at the SIEM level (e.g., Splunk transaction, Elastic EQL sequence) as Sigma does not natively support temporal cross-log correlation. 

            <h3>7.3 Network Segmentation</h3>

            <p>The single most effective mitigation against ransomware cascade within semiconductor environments is
                <strong>strict IT/OT segmentation</strong>. Given that CloudSEK's data shows 60% of OT breaches
                originate from IT-side vulnerabilities, the boundary between corporate IT and fab/manufacturing OT
                must be treated as a hard perimeter:
            </p>

            <ul>
                <li>Deploy unidirectional security gateways (data diodes) at IT/OT boundaries.</li>
                <li>Prohibit direct RDP, SMB, and WMI traffic from corporate networks to OT zones.</li>
                <li>Maintain separate Active Directory forests for IT and OT environments.</li>
                <li>Implement network-level micro-segmentation around EDA (Electronic Design Automation)
                    workstations containing chip design IP.</li>
            </ul>

            <div class="success-box">
                <h3><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> IMMEDIATE ACTIONS for Semiconductor Companies</h3>
                <ul>
                    <li><strong>Audit VPN and remote access:</strong> Disable all unused VPN accounts. Enforce MFA
                        on every remote access point.</li>
                    <li><strong>Segment IT from OT:</strong> Ensure no direct path exists from corporate email
                        endpoints to manufacturing control systems.</li>
                    <li><strong>Backup verification:</strong> Test offline backup restoration procedures. Ensure
                        backups are immutable and air-gapped.</li>
                    <li><strong>Incident response readiness:</strong> Conduct a tabletop exercise specifically
                        modeling a ransomware attack on your EDA or test infrastructure.</li>
                    <li><strong>CIRCIA preparation:</strong> Register for the March 12, 2026 CISA town hall for
                        Critical Manufacturing. Begin documenting your incident reporting procedures.</li>
                </ul>
            </div>

            <!-- FAQ Section -->
            <div class="faq-container"
                style="margin-top: 4rem; padding: 2rem; background: var(--bg-secondary); border-radius: 12px; border: 1px solid var(--border);">

                <div class="faq-item" style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;">
                    <h4 style="color: #fff; font-size: 1.2rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem;">What happened to Advantest?
                    </h4>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin-top: 0;">On February 15, 2026, Advantest
                        Corporation detected a ransomware attack on its IT network. The company isolated affected
                        systems and engaged forensic investigators. As of February 25, 2026, no data breach has been
                        confirmed and no ransomware group has publicly claimed responsibility. Sources: <a
                            href="https://www.securityweek.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
                            style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">SecurityWeek</a>, <a
                            href="https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
                            style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">BleepingComputer</a>.</p>
                </div>

                <div class="faq-item" style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;">
                    <h4 style="color: #fff; font-size: 1.2rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem;">Does the CHIPS Act fund
                        cybersecurity?</h4>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin-top: 0;">The CHIPS Act allocates $500 million to
                        the International Technology Security and Innovation (ITSI) Fund, administered by the State
                        Department. This fund supports international supply chain diversification and secure telecom
                        — not domestic ransomware defense for semiconductor manufacturers. Source: <a
                            href="https://www.state.gov/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">U.S.
                            Department of State</a>.</p>
                </div>

                <div class="faq-item" style="margin-bottom: 1.5rem;">
                    <h4 style="color: #fff; font-size: 1.2rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem;">How much has the
                        semiconductor industry lost to ransomware?</h4>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin-top: 0;">CloudSEK's threat report documents over
                        $1.05 billion in confirmed ransomware losses across the semiconductor industry since 2018,
                        with a 600%+ surge in attacks since 2022. Individual incidents include $200M (MKS
                        Instruments), $250M downstream (Applied Materials), and $21.4M (Microchip Technology).
                        Sources: <a href="https://www.csoonline.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
                            style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">CSO Online</a>, <a
                            href="https://www.securityweek.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
                            style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">SecurityWeek</a>.</p>
                </div>

                <div class="faq-item">
                    <h4 style="color: #fff; font-size: 1.2rem; margin-bottom: 0.5rem;">What is CIRCIA and when does
                        it take effect?</h4>
                    <p style="color: var(--text-secondary); margin-top: 0;">The Cyber Incident Reporting for
                        Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022 (CIRCIA) will require critical infrastructure entities —
                        including semiconductor manufacturers — to report cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours
                        and ransomware payments within 24 hours. The final rule is expected by May 2026. CISA is
                        holding <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/circia" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"
                            style="color: var(--accent-cyan);">virtual town halls in March 2026</a> to gather
                        stakeholder input.</p>
                </div>
            </div>
